EMT now and again the complacency of the people who are for " letting well alone" suffers a momentary shock. Sayings and doings which difler materially from those seedbed to the 'contented poor" in parish magazines crop out, oecasionally, and reveal an amount of ignorance and credulity such as would have disgraced a fax less highly. developed civilization than that which we make our boast. The fortune-telling cases recently adjudicated upon in Liverpool afford an apt illustration of the chronic liability to fall into the practice of debasing supersti. Mom, which is, and always has been, the characteristic of the popular mind. We feli- citate ourselves sometimes upon the rapid advance of intelligence in this country. We point to our reforms and extensions of edu- cational machinery. And, no doubt, there has been a very wide diffusion of ideas within the memory of the generation that in dying out. But, after all, how little has been ac- complished compared with the work that still waits achievement. Thus, it is in evidence that mires of women and girls besieged the house in which Mary bleeding—" an old and very feeble-looking' person—gave audi- ence, at • shilling apiece. Wiry Monday should be" a busy day with the fortune- tellers' dow not quite appear. Mary Mas- sey and Mary City appeared to have favoured tea-leaves as media of divination, as well as cards. The former told one of the witnesses that "her husband was jealous, that he would go away, and that she would I leave her situation in • few mouths," She also said that there was some little woman who tried to crush witness down." Another testified that the prisoner "said she oould tell her temper by means of the line. in her hand..' Thu kind of thing is evidently quite common amongst the lower class in our towns and villages. Does it not suggest • few painful reflections? It ia clear that heat enism in • deeper sense than the term usually implies is rampant incur midet. It is equally clear that the forms and symbols of sectarian Christianity do not touch the mites of our population. And yet there are churches and chapels in plenty , priests and portions hard at work, commending their various interpretations of the Bible and the Hospel. What lack we yet? Surely the evils which still have their strength in the popular mind are such as only "sound know- ledge and discretion" can expel. Religion itself is a hindrance and not a help to mural development when it fosters magical arts and superstitious terrors and tangles. What frightful things it can sanction we may learn from impartial history; and, indeed, may witness on a gigantic scale in the Emit. even now. There is no permanent help to be found save in the enlightenment Which follow a in the wake of scientific and literary culture. We are not taping that thedf.. comprehend all elevating knowledge ; we are oit!y emphasizing a fact which is be- coming more and more patent . to thoughtful philanthropists--a fact which Kingsley urged upon his hearers and readers just as strenuously as Huxley doee—vir., that the raw religious sentiments need more, and not less, the guidance and restraint which spring out of the knowledge of the workings of natural law, just because they are the strongest and the moat venerable. An earnest bigot is like a locomotive which has escaped control. He will dare or do any. I thing under the impulse of misdirected seal. And as to the low, ignorant, almost brutal , residuum of our population—we are driven: to despair of any reformation which does not take its :lee in the school. and in the univer- sal spread of simple and sound ideas about moral duty and its relation to human happi- ness. The man who has net begun to live intellectually has hardly begun to live as • human being at all. Be is at the mercy of every charlatan. He is, consequently, a care to his intelligent neighbours, just am much as the inmate of the County Asylum is —nay, he may be more costly and trouble- some, for he enjoys a liberty which is often dangerous to himself and others. By all means let the magistrate and the policeman come down upon the wretches who trade up- on the ignorant hopes and fears of the people; but let the ruling pleases also feel their responsibility. Let them neglect no means of spreading enlightened views of life and the world; especially aiding every •ffort to make the poor more thoughtful and ,;-.qmr. 7. As a matter of economic policy this cow!. oug 'acon.unend itself more and li,' more; aa a duty which tn.::: owe t°, thl't favoured brethren they must sure;, in time, give it their first and not their lam consider- ation. There is no safety in a program which is not intellectual and moral, as well as material. These choked drains want clearing also; light is needed in the mind ae well as in the dwelling; the wholesome and invigorating air of knowledge must be breathed by the masses, or our national life will be an arreated development, and ow vaunted leadership will—like that of the nations of antiquity—for ever pass away into more faithful hands.

A terrible battle has been raging in the Shipka Pane for more than • week, and the Ottoman Commander, Suleiman Pasha, has poured enormous reinforcements into the Pass, and made frightful sacrifices of men and material, in the desperate hope of rout- ing the Russian. who are in possession. It , would appear that the Russian re- serves have not moved to the scene of struggle with the ceierity that was an- ticipated and the contlict has had to be waged by the Rusaian troops under unex- pected disadvantages. Telegraphic rumour I —as usual—has worn the chamelion com- plexion especially common to military rumour, where the seat of notion in remote, I and the history of the hour is difficult of correction. The tremendous struggle in the Pass has been represented as an unexampled disaster to the Russian arms, and as the loss of an invaluable military position. The latest accounts fail to verify this version of the war narrative. There can be no doubt that Suleiman Pasha has staked all his available forms, and that the courage of both Turks and Russians has never been more conspicuous. It is needless to add that the slaughter has been frightful. It now , ; seems certain that in spite of the superhuman efforts of the Turkish troops the Russians ; maintain their position. The despatch ad- dressed to the War Olhes at Constantinople ; len Sunday evening by Suleiman says I that his soldiers up to that time had ; I been engaged for six days in uninterrupted ' fighting. The result he states to be the oc- eupation by. his troops of the heights of Alikrid Jebel, on the Russian left, which command the enemy's line of retreat. The enemy's formidable works had not been I taken, and thus the issue of the combat was not decided. The greater part of the de- spatch is taken up with a description of the struggle for the possession of Alikrid Jebel. On oaturdey, he nays, the Russian troops made continual assaults from morning till evening, replacing or reinforcing the attack- ing columns by fresh troops. About four o'clock in the afternoon three Russian com- panies succeeded in making their way into the position, but the first and third Turkish brigades, under Vessel Patina, partly re- occupied them. The fighting continued all night, and at three o'clock on Sunday morn- ing the Turkish troop. had completely driven out the enemy, and at daybreak reoccupied all the positions. The Russians, receiving reinforcements on Sunday morning, unsuc- ()woefully attempted a final assault, after which they returned to their fortitied works. The cannonade continued all Sunday, with- out appreciable result. In the Russian official report it is stated that since Monday evening the musketry lire in the Pass had almost ceased; and on Tuesday morning all was quiet, the Russian troops maintaining their former positions. The Turks remained under cover, and out of reach of the Russian batteries. The chief of the Russian stall has been cent to inspect the Russian position in the Pam. The total number of wounded fromthe 2lst to the 27th ult. is 2,410, including 93 officers. The sur- geons and their amistants, aided by the staff of the Red Cross Society, work with great activity and devotion. The wounded are being taken from Gabrova. The Russian loss in dead is returned as not being known. Of the future intentions of both armies nothing M empire., but the correspondent of the Daily IN't ics reports that the ituseians have been adequately reinforced, and he sees no reason to alter his opinion previously ex- pressed, that General liadetiky has a safe hold of the position. The same correspond- ent in Suleiman Pitches camp states that the country at the southern foot of the Balkans is being desolated by one belligerent or other, or, failing them, by the Bulgarians, every village is burned down, and the population has fled. "Wherever Suleiman goes ruin and desolation follow at his heels, but he appears only acting under orders in permit- I I ting it." This correspondent was confidently assured that all the inhabitants of • Turkish I village near his route had been massacred by the Bulgarian insurgents ; but instead of tele- graphing the fact he inquired into it, and ; ' found that there was not • word of truth in ; ; the report. It cannot be hoped that the Turkish men- , dacity will know any abatement so long as it is likely to influence in ever so small a degree European opinion to its advantage. One thing seems to become clearer every ' day, and that is that this horrible war can- not be closed during the present year, un- less, as appears to the last degree unlikely, the Powers should be able to devise some scheme of mediation, and impose the will of Europe on the belligerents in the interest of civilisation.
